java-core.title: Java Core
java-core.blurb: The building blocks of the Java language — objects, classes, and how to handle things going wrong.

OOP (Object-Oriented Programming): A way of structuring code around "objects" that bundle data and behavior together.
Think of a car: it has data (color, speed) and behavior (drive, brake) bundled into one thing — that's an object.
Every Java program you'll ever write is built from objects — this is the foundation everything else sits on.
Grown-ups like to keep toys organized in toy boxes. OOP means putting a computer's information and its actions into one box called an object, so everything stays together and easy to find.
Class: A blueprint/template for creating objects (defines fields and methods).
A class is like a cookie cutter — it's not a cookie itself, it's the shape used to make cookies.
You write the class once, then create as many objects from it as you need.
A class is like a coloring book page before you color it in — it shows the shape, but it is not a real picture yet.
Object: A specific instance created from a class.
If Dog is the cookie cutter, then 'Rex' the actual dog is the cookie — one real thing made from the shape.
The `new` keyword is what actually builds an object from a class.
An object is the picture after you have colored it in — a real one made from the coloring page, which is the class.
Inheritance: A class reusing/extending the fields and methods of another class.
A Puppy is a kind of Dog — it gets everything a Dog has for free, plus its own extras.
Inheritance keeps you from copy-pasting the same code into every related class.
It is like a little brother getting hand-me-down clothes from his big brother — he gets everything big brother had, and can add his own stuff too.
Interface: A contract listing methods a class must implement, without saying how.
An interface is like a job posting — it lists what the job requires, but each hire does the work their own way.
Interfaces let unrelated classes promise to behave the same way, which makes code far more flexible.
It is like a promise list: "I promise I can jump, run, and swim" — but it does not say exactly how you do each one.
Encapsulation: Keeping an object's internal data private and exposing controlled access via methods.
Think of a vending machine: you can't reach in and grab a snack directly — you press a button and it hands it to you safely.

private double balance;
public double getBalance() { return balance; }
This is how you protect data from being changed in ways that break your program.
It is like a piggy bank. You can put coins in and take coins out through the slot, but you cannot just reach inside and grab things any way you want.
Exception: An error event that interrupts normal program flow.
It's the code equivalent of tripping mid-sentence — something unexpected happened and the normal flow stops.
Exceptions aren't failures of your code — they're Java's way of telling you exactly what went wrong.
It is like tripping over your shoelace while walking — something unexpected happens and you have to stop and deal with it.
Try / Catch / Finally: The block structure used to attempt risky code, handle its errors, and clean up afterward.
Try = attempt the risky move. Catch = the safety net if it fails. Finally = happens no matter what, like closing a door behind you.
`finally` runs even if you return early or an exception escapes — great for closing files or connections.

Try is attempting something a little risky, like walking on a balance beam. Catch is the net that catches you if you fall. Finally happens no matter what, like always putting your shoes away when you are done.
Checked vs. Unchecked Exception: Checked exceptions must be declared/handled at compile time; unchecked ones (like RuntimeException) don't have to be.
Checked = the compiler forces you to plan for it ahead of time. Unchecked = it can surprise you at runtime.
If the compiler is yelling at you about an exception, it's checked. If your program just crashes, it was unchecked.
A checked exception is like a grown-up reminding you to bring an umbrella before it rains. An unchecked one is like it starts raining and surprises you.
Collection (List/Map/Set): Built-in Java data structures for storing groups of objects.
A List is a numbered line, a Set is a bag with no duplicates allowed, and a Map is a labeled set of drawers.
Picking the right collection (List vs Set vs Map) is one of the most common early design decisions.
A List is like a line of kids holding hands in order. A Set is a group where no two kids can be exactly the same. A Map is like cubbies with each kid's name taped on.
JDK / JRE / JVM: JDK = tools to build Java apps. JRE = what's needed to run them. JVM = the engine that actually executes the compiled code.
JDK is the whole workshop (tools + parts), JRE is just the finished machine, and the JVM is the engine inside that machine actually running.

javac Hello.java   // JDK compiles
java Hello          // JVM runs the compiled bytecode
You need the JDK to develop; end users only need the JRE (or just a JVM) to run your finished app.
The JDK is the whole toolbox for building toys. The JRE is just what you need to play with a toy someone already built. The JVM is the little engine inside that actually makes the toy move.

spring-boot.title: Spring Boot
spring-boot.blurb: How to build a real, working REST API in Java — controllers, services, repositories, and the database.

Spring Boot: A framework that simplifies building Java web applications with sensible defaults.
Spring Boot is like a furnished apartment instead of an empty lot — the plumbing and wiring are already done for you.
That one `main` method is all it takes to start a full working web server.
It is like a toy that comes already put together, instead of one you have to build piece by piece yourself.
Controller: Receives incoming HTTP requests and returns responses; the "front door" of the API.
The Controller is the receptionist — it greets every request coming in and routes it to the right place.
If you're wondering "what URL does this hit?" — the answer lives in a Controller.
It is like the person at the front desk of a school who greets you and tells you which room to go to.
Service: Holds the business logic — the "what should happen" layer, called by the Controller.
If the Controller is the receptionist, the Service is the manager who actually decides what to do with the request.
Keeping logic in the Service (not the Controller) makes your code much easier to test and reuse.
It is the teacher in that room who actually decides what you will do and helps you do it.
Repository: Handles talking to the database (queries, saves, deletes) — usually via Spring Data JPA.
The Repository is the filing clerk — it's the only layer that actually touches the file cabinet (the database).
Spring Data can generate basic save/find/delete methods for you — you barely have to write any SQL.
It is the librarian who goes and gets the exact book you asked for from the shelves.
REST API: An API style using standard HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) and URLs to represent resources.
REST is like a well-labeled filing system: every "thing" has an address (URL), and you use a small, consistent set of verbs to act on it.

GET /tasks       // read all
POST /tasks      // create one
PUT /tasks/3     // update one
DELETE /tasks/3  // delete one
Once you know REST conventions, you can guess how almost any well-designed API works.
It is like a menu at a restaurant. You point at what you want, and there is one simple way to ask for it, get it, change it, or send it back.
Endpoint: A specific URL + HTTP method combination the API responds to (e.g. GET /tasks).
An endpoint is one specific counter at a service desk — one exact combination of "where" and "what kind of request."
Every button or screen in a front-end app is usually backed by one or more endpoints like this.
It is one exact spot on the menu, like "small hot chocolate" — a very specific thing you can order.
@RestController / @Autowired: Annotations: the first marks a class as an API controller; the second injects a needed dependency automatically.
Annotations are sticky notes on your code that tell Spring "treat this specially."
`@Autowired` means you never have to write `new TaskService()` yourself — Spring hands it to you.
These are like little name tags that tell your class "hey, you're the front desk" or "you'll be handed the toy you need automatically."
Dependency Injection (DI): A pattern where objects get the other objects they need handed to them, instead of creating them internally.
Instead of a chef growing their own vegetables, someone delivers exactly what's needed to the kitchen door.
DI is what makes Spring apps so testable — you can swap in fake dependencies for testing.
Instead of making your own lunch every day, someone hands you a lunch box that is already packed with what you need.
Entity: A Java class mapped directly to a database table.
An Entity is a mirror image of one row-shape in your database, written as a Java class.
Every field in an @Entity usually becomes a column in a database table.
It is like a trading card that matches exactly one drawer in a filing cabinet — the card's info matches the drawer's info.
JPA / Hibernate: The standard (JPA) and popular implementation (Hibernate) for mapping Java objects to database rows (ORM).
JPA is the rulebook for translating Java objects into database rows; Hibernate is the translator that actually does the work.

taskRepository.save(new Task("Buy milk"));
// Hibernate turns this into an INSERT statement for you
This is why you rarely have to write raw SQL when using Spring Data JPA.
It is a helper who takes your toy blocks and neatly puts them away in the toy chest (the database) for you.
DTO (Data Transfer Object): A simple object used to shape data sent between layers or over the API, separate from the database Entity.
A DTO is like a gift-wrapped version of your data — you don't hand someone the whole warehouse, just the box they asked for.
DTOs let you hide sensitive or irrelevant fields before sending data out over the API.
It is like a gift box — you only put in what you want to share, not your whole room.
HTTP Status Codes: Numeric response codes, e.g. 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error.
Status codes are like traffic lights on every response — a quick signal for whether things went well before you even read the details.
2xx = success, 4xx = you (the client) made a mistake, 5xx = the server made a mistake.
They are like traffic lights: green (200) means success, yellow-ish (400) means you made a mistake, red (500) means something broke on their end.
application.properties / .yml: The config file where you set database connections, ports, and other app settings.
This file is the settings panel for your whole app — one place to tune how it behaves without touching code.
Changing this file (not your Java code) is usually how you point the same app at a different database.
It is like the settings page on a game console — you can change things like the volume without changing the game itself.

angular.title: Angular
angular.blurb: The front-end framework that turns your API's data into an interactive page people actually use.

TypeScript: A typed superset of JavaScript that compiles down to plain JavaScript, used as Angular's language.
TypeScript is JavaScript with a spellchecker built in — it catches type mistakes before your code ever runs.
Those `: number` and `: string` labels are what let your editor warn you before you even hit save.
It is like writing with a pencil that has a little alarm. If you try to write "5" where a word should go, it beeps before you finish, so you can fix it early.
Component: A self-contained UI building block: template (HTML) + logic (TypeScript) + styles (CSS).
A component is like a Lego brick for your page — a self-contained piece you can snap in anywhere and reuse.

@Component({ selector: 'app-task', templateUrl: './task.html' })
export class TaskComponent { title = 'My Task'; }
Almost everything you see on an Angular page — a button, a card, a whole page — is a component.
It is one Lego piece — a button, a card, a little box — that you can snap onto your page.
Service: A reusable class (usually for logic like fetching data) shared across components via dependency injection.
If components are the stage actors, a Service is the shared script and props room everyone pulls from.
Put data-fetching logic in a Service, not in the Component — it keeps your components focused on display.
It is a helper who runs and fetches things for lots of different Lego pieces, so they do not each have to fetch it themselves.
Module: A container that groups related components, services, and other code together.
A module is like a chapter folder in a binder — it groups related pieces so Angular knows how they fit together.
Newer Angular apps increasingly use "standalone" components instead, but modules are still common in existing projects.
It is like a toy bin that holds a bunch of related Lego pieces together in one group.
Data Binding: Connecting data in the component's TypeScript to the HTML template so they stay in sync.
Data binding is like a two-way mirror between your code and your screen — change one side, the other updates.
This is why Angular apps feel so "live" — you rarely have to manually update the DOM yourself.
It is like a magic notebook — write something on one page, and it shows up on the matching page too, automatically.
Directive: Instructions attached to HTML elements to change their behavior or appearance (e.g. *ngIf, *ngFor).
A directive is a command whispered to an HTML tag, telling it to show/hide, repeat, or behave differently.

• {{ task.title }}

    • No tasks yet
`*ngFor` and `*ngIf` are the two directives you'll use constantly when displaying lists of data.
It is a sticky note stuck to a Lego piece that says "only show me if this is true" or "repeat me for every item in the list."
Routing / Router: The system that maps URLs to different components, enabling navigation without full page reloads.
The router is like a building directory — it decides which "room" (component) to show based on the address typed in.
This is what makes Angular apps feel like multiple pages while staying a single fast-loading app.
It is like a hallway with room numbers — typing a different address takes you to a different room without leaving the building.
HttpClient: Angular's built-in tool for making HTTP requests to a backend API.
HttpClient is Angular's phone line to your Spring Boot backend — it's how the two sides actually talk.
This single line is usually how your Angular front end pulls in real data from your REST API.
It is the walkie-talkie your app uses to call the kitchen (the server) and ask for food (data).
Observable / Subscribe: A stream of data over time; you 'subscribe' to react whenever new data arrives.
An Observable is like signing up for a newsletter — you don't get one email, you get notified every time new content arrives.
Nothing happens with an Observable until something subscribes to it — that's the key mental model.
It is like signing up for a cereal-box club. You do not get anything right away, but every time something new comes out, they send it to you.
npm / Angular CLI: npm manages JavaScript packages; the Angular CLI scaffolds and manages Angular projects from the command line.
npm is the app store for code libraries; the Angular CLI is the power tool that builds your project's scaffolding for you.

ng generate component task-list
npm install
ng serve
`ng serve` is usually the first command you run to see your Angular app live in the browser.
npm is like a toy store where you can download tools other people built. The Angular CLI is a robot helper that builds the basic toy structure for you so you do not start from a blank table.

rest-git.title: REST, Git & General
rest-git.blurb: The glue that ties everything together — how the front end and back end talk, and how your team tracks code.

API (Application Programming Interface): A defined way for one piece of software to talk to another.
An API is a restaurant menu — you don't need to know how the kitchen works, you just order from the menu and get a result.

// Calling an API from Angular
this.http.get('/api/tasks')
Every time an app "talks" to another service, an API is the contract making that possible.
It is a menu. You do not need to know how the kitchen cooks, you just order from the list.
JSON: A lightweight text format for exchanging structured data, used heavily by REST APIs.
JSON is like a neatly labeled shipping box — data packed in a structured, predictable way anyone can unpack.
Nearly every REST API request and response body you'll see is JSON.
It is like a neatly labeled lunchbox — everything has its own labeled spot, so whoever opens it knows exactly what is what.
Client-Server: The architecture where a client (e.g. Angular app) requests data/services from a server (e.g. Spring Boot API).
It's a customer (client) placing an order at a counter (server) — the client asks, the server fulfills.
Angular (client) --HTTP request--> Spring Boot (server) --JSON response--> Angular
This split is exactly why your front end and back end can be built and deployed completely separately.
The client is you asking for a snack, and the server is the grown-up in the kitchen who gets it for you.
CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four basic operations most applications perform on data.
CRUD is the four things you can do to almost anything in a filing cabinet: add it, look at it, change it, or toss it.

POST /tasks    -> Create
GET /tasks     -> Read
PUT /tasks/1   -> Update
DELETE /tasks/1 -> Delete
If you can build clean CRUD, you can build the backbone of almost any application.
It is the four things you can do with your toys: get a new one, look at it, change it, or throw it away.
Repository (Git): A storage location (local or remote, like GitHub) that tracks the history of a project's files.
A Git repository is a project's diary — every change ever made is saved, dated, and never truly lost.

git init
git remote add origin https://github.com/you/project.git
Everything about your project's history lives inside the `.git` folder of a repository.
It is a treasure chest that remembers every version of your drawing, even the really old, silly ones.
Commit: A saved snapshot of changes in Git, with a message describing what changed.
A commit is a save point in a video game — you can always come back to exactly this moment later.

git add .
git commit -m "Add task delete endpoint"
Small, frequent commits with clear messages make your work easy to review and easy to undo if needed.
It is like taking a photo of your Lego tower right now, so you can always look back and see exactly how it looked.
Branch: A parallel line of development in Git, used to work on features without affecting the main codebase.
A branch is a separate scratch copy of the project — you can experiment freely without messing up the original.
Working on a branch means your changes are safely isolated until you're ready to merge them in.
It is like making a copy of your drawing so you can try adding a wild new color without messing up the original.
Pull Request (PR): A request to merge changes from one branch into another, usually with review from teammates.
A pull request is like turning in a draft for peer review before it becomes the official final version.
# On GitHub: open a PR from feature/add-login -> main
PRs are where most real-world code review and team feedback happens.
It is like raising your hand and asking a grown-up, "can I add my new drawing to the class art wall?" before it goes up.
Merge / Merge Conflict: Merge combines changes from branches; a conflict happens when the same lines were changed differently.
A merge conflict is like two people editing the same sentence in a shared document at once — Git needs you to decide which version wins.

git merge feature/add-login
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in TaskService.java
Conflicts aren't errors to fear — they're just Git asking you to make the final call.
Merging is putting two kids' drawings together into one picture. A conflict is when they both drew something different in the exact same spot, so someone has to pick.
Clone / Push / Pull: Clone copies a remote repo locally; push sends local commits to the remote; pull fetches and merges remote changes.
Clone = get your own copy. Push = mail your changes out. Pull = pick up everyone else's mail.

git clone https://github.com/you/project.git
git push origin main
git pull origin main
Pulling before you push is a habit that saves you from a lot of avoidable merge conflicts.
Clone is making your own copy of the class treasure chest. Push is adding your new toys to it. Pull is grabbing the newest toys everyone else added.
